    How this is coded

    Select a mark to see the quote and source.

    Select a country to see its functions, then a function for its quote and source.

    We read each institute's founding, legal and plan texts and its own published work, and recorded a function only where a quote meets that function's test. Active: a public text reports the institute doing it. Assigned: a government text gives it the function. Most recent coding: 14 Nov 2026. Each institute's values are in functions.csv and claims.csv under Data.

    'Active since at least' is the date of the oldest published text in which we found this work. We leave the date out when we know of older work that we have not added yet.

    Rows: by the year the institute's current status began, oldest first.

    The list of functions is provisional.

    Canada: Funding and staff recordsCanada, Canadian AI Safety Institute

    Budget

    ~EUR 6.3m (CAD 10m)a year average over period 2024-25 to 2028-29 adopted ~EUR 0.15 per resident (2025)1,2,3

    Staff

    Not published

    Own funding

    ~EUR 32m (CAD 50m) multi-year 2024-25 to 2028-29 adopted1,2,3

    Source statement

    CAD 50m over five years

    Component: Contributions to CIFAR for CAISI's applied and investigator-led research stream, 2024-25 to 2028-29: CAD 2,999,545 actual spending in 2024-25 (funding received in-year, none planned), CAD 6m actual spending in 2025-26 and CAD 6m planned for each later year.4,5,6,7

    ~EUR 17m (~CAD 27m) multi-year 2024-25 to 2028-29 (2024-25 and 2025-26 actual spending, later years planned spending) announced3,4,5,6,7

    Source statement

    Contributions to CIFAR for CAISI's applied and investigator-led research stream, 2024-25 to 2028-29: CAD 2,999,545 actual spending in 2024-25 (funding received in-year, none planned), CAD 6m actual spending in 2025-26 and CAD 6m planned for each later year.4,5,6,7

    ISED's 2026-27 Departmental Plan lists the CAISI project under the Advanced and Emerging Technology programme with a start of 2024-25 and an end of 2028-29 (CAISI Budget 2024), as does its 2025-26 results report, so this stream sits inside the CAD 50m five-year allocation and is not additional to it. ISED's 2024-25 results report and its 2025-26 Departmental Plan give the start as 2025-26, but the 2024-25 results report also records CAD 2,999,545 of actual spending in 2024-25 against nothing planned, as funding received in-year, and says the stream was launched in November 2024; the record therefore starts in 2024-25. ISED's 2025-26 Departmental Results Report gives CAD 6m as 2025-26 actual spending (authorities used), equal to planned spending. CIFAR reported on 21 January 2026 that the government awarded it CAD 27m through the institute for its AI safety research programme, with no period stated, and that the programme awarded CAD 2.4m in 2025 to 12 projects; both concern this stream and are not added to it.4,5,6,7,8

    ~EUR 32m (CAD 50m) one-off announced3,9,10

    Source statement

    An additional CAD 50m announced through AI for All to expand CAISI capabilities.9,10

    The retrieved sources publish no funding period or annual profile, so we do not annualise it, do not use it in place of the 2024 five-year allocation, and do not add the two envelopes to a current annual budget. The one-off label denotes this additional fixed envelope, not payment in one fiscal year. The strategy names CAISI as the recipient, and the Question Period Note explicitly calls this additional funding. It is an institute-wide envelope, kept separate from the earlier five-year allocation rather than added to its annual mean. The Question Period Note also associates the envelope with AI transparency and a Canada Trusted AI Certification programme. It gives no split; the explicit CAISI allocation supports the whole-institute classification while the scope of certification spending remains uncertain.9,10

    Japan: Funding and staff recordsJapan, Japan AI Safety Institute

    Staff

    311

    as of Apr 2026

    Own funding

    ~EUR 52m (JPY 8.8bn) one-off FY2025 supplementary adopted1,2

    Stated purposes include AI evaluation methods, dedicated testbeds and compute. Includes work commissioned to AIST on safety research, guidelines and international standardisation for robots working with people, not model evaluation. The Cabinet Office assigns the full package to strengthening AISI and says AISI itself develops evaluation tools. The AIST commission is listed within that package, so the total is treated as AISI's own funding, not a separate host programme or recurring annual spending. The source does not identify the appropriation recipient for every part.1

    ~EUR 2.2m (JPY 380m) one-off FY2024 supplementary adopted1,2

    The Cabinet Office comparison lists this amount in Japan AISI's budget cell, so it is treated as the institute's own allocation. It is not recurring annual spending.1

    Staff records

    The 7 April 2026 Cabinet Office document's comparison table gives 31 including concurrent appointments from IPA and RIKEN. The target of 60 is from a governing-party (LDP) recommendation of 19 December 2025 that the document reproduces, which asks to expand urgently from the then current 30; a separate government plan has ministries second staff from April to around July 2026. The prime minister's instruction of 19 December 2025 aims for 200, with no target date stated. The count is the one the document gives as current in April 2026, its publication month; it states no separate headcount date. as of Apr 20261

    Just over 30 staff including concurrent appointments within IPA, of whom 20 are dedicated staff. The lower-bound total is not a dedicated-only count. as of Jan 20263

    The government plans 13 secondments from ministries at assistant or section-chief level on 1-2 year terms. A governing-party (LDP) recommendation asks that the institute be allowed to pay above civil-service scales.

    Suggest a correction

    Established institutes only; planned and proposed ones are in their own records. Budget bars compare committed funding for 2026. Staff bars show dated totals; dates and qualifications differ.

    How this is chosen

    Budget bars share one scale and show adopted or announced funding for the whole institute in a funding year that overlaps 2026, the calendar year of the data date. Where several years qualify, the one containing the data date is used, if there is one. Proposals, one-off amounts and other years keep their amounts in the records. Components are excluded from the comparison. Period means are named in the figure explanations and the records. EUR figures are rough conversions at the ECB's 2025 annual-average rates and do not compare like with like. Staff bars have their own scale and show published totals with dates. Dates, bounds and commitments are explained on hover, focus or tap on a figure; the same explanation is available to screen readers. Bounds and approximations also stay on the number as up to, ~ or +. Technical counts, targets and ranges remain in the records and do not become total bars.

    DataDownloads Method

    Data

    Download

    The data behind this page is free to reuse under CC BY 4.0, with attribution.

    Start here CSV

    • States and territoriesjurisdictions.csvstatus, dates and region of every state and territory, and the EU
    • Institutesinstitutes.csvhost, form, mandate and website of each institute
    • All eventsevents.csvdated government acts, agreements, outputs and network milestones
    • Newsnews.csvnews entries with dates, states, institutes, kinds and sources

    Institutes CSV

    • Staffstaff.csvheadcounts, technical staff and targets, dated
    • Fundingfunding.csvpublished funding amounts, periods and annual EUR estimates
    • Leadershippeople.csvheads and leads of each institute
    • Outputsoutputs.csvpublications, tools and datasets credited to each institute
    • Agreementsagreements.csvcommitments made with AI developers, governments and other institutes
    • National partnersnational_partners.csvnational partner bodies and their work with each institute
    • Known activityknown_activity.csvthe earliest published work and joint testing of each institute
    • Functionsfunctions.csvfunction codes and values for each institute, with supporting claims; codes are provisional

    States CSV

    • Status timelinetimeline.csvthe dated government acts that set each status
    • Closest candidatesclosest_bodies.csvfor states with none identified, the nearest body and what it lacks
    • Related bodiesrelated_bodies.csvAI Act authorities and other bodies not counted as institutes
    • Network milestonesnetwork_milestones.csvfounding, meetings and renaming of the international network

    Evidence CSV

    • Sourcessources.csvevery source with publisher, date and archive link
    • Source excerptssource_excerpts.csvthe quoted passages and the values they support
    • Claimsclaims.csvquoted claims on states and institutes: one sentence, its code and its sources
    • Exchange ratesexchange_rates.csvthe ECB rates used for the EUR figures

    For code JSON

    • Full datasetaisi.jsonevery record with its sources, confidence and check dates
    • Schemaaisi.schema.jsonfield definitions and validation rules
    • Data packagedatapackage.jsonfile list, formats and table schemas
    • Consistency checksshared-claim-coverage.jsonrepeated figures and the checks that compare them

    For programs and agents

    • API indexapi/v1/index.jsonAn index of the state and institute JSON files
    • llms.txtllms.txtA plain-text guide to the data for AI agents
    • Feedfeed.xmlNews and releases in Atom format

    Method

    We count a body as an AI Security Institute (AISI) if a national government or an international organisation, such as the EU, has tasked it with testing general-purpose or frontier AI models for their capabilities and risks, or has named it its AI safety institute or its AI security institute. Being a regulator, certification body or cyber security agency is not enough on its own. The test in detail

    Status, evidence and method

    Status definitions

    • Established. A national government or an international organisation, such as the EU, has created or designated a body to test general-purpose or frontier AI models for their capabilities and risks, or has named a body as its AI safety institute or its AI security institute.
    • Planned. The government has adopted a commitment to create or designate a named body with that task or that name.
    • Proposed. The government has formally proposed such a body, and approval is pending.
    • Exploring. The government is studying or drafting plans for such a body, or a government-appointed advisory commission has recommended one.
    • None identified. Our searches found no current government decision, commitment, formal proposal, study, draft plan or government-appointed advisory recommendation for such a body.

    Method in brief

    • Testing general-purpose or frontier AI models distinguishes an AI Security Institute from an AI regulator or digital ministry. We set no minimum size, because budgets and staff differ too much between countries, and report them separately. Full rule
    • Population comes from Eurostat for the 32 European states, the World Bank for the rest and Taiwan's Ministry of the Interior for Taiwan. Regions follow the UN's M49 grouping, with Taiwan placed in Eastern Asia. Full rules on Population of European states and Population outside the 32 European states
    • An empty value means not known or not published. It never means zero or no. Full rule
    • Known activity, shown only for established institutes and separately from status, gives the earliest published evaluation or other technical work credited to the institute by name and the earliest joint testing it took part in. Finding none is not evidence of inactivity. Full rule
    • A check date records a full re-check against the sources. Where the original log is lost, it gives the latest day by which the check happened, which may be later than the check itself. Full rule
    • Confidence describes the strength of the evidence for a status. None identified is a finding of our searches, not proof that nothing exists. Full rule
    • Key claims are backed by short quotations from their sources, with our English translations where needed. Review checks whether the quotations support the claims. Full rule
    • An output counts when the institute wrote it or is credited with it as its own work, with versions of one document counted once. Its first output is the earliest item credited to it, including network reports that name it. Full rules on Outputs and First output
    • We count the days from a government's first announcement or proposal to the institute's establishment, and from establishment to the first documented qualifying work credited to it. A date known only to the month or year gives a range, which stays in the downloads. The intervals are not a ranking, because the announcing act and the kind of body differ between states. Full rule
    • An agreement counts when the institute is a named party or a government agreement names it as the body carrying it out. Company pledges are recorded separately from signed agreements. Full rule
    • A card shows the institute's own funding for the year that includes the data date, otherwise the latest adopted or announced amount, and failing that the latest proposal. The chart compares adopted or announced whole-institute funding for a year overlapping the data year, while wider funding is shown as Related funding. Full rules on Annual funding and Budget display
    • Where a national act in force differs from the European Commission's list, we follow the national act. A pending proposal is not a designation. Full rule
    • For a claim about a state or its institute we cite that state's own primary source first, in any language, and add an English source where one exists. Where we found only another country's account, the entry says who reported it. Full rule
    • Non-English source titles are shown in our own English translation; the original title appears on hover, focus and tap. Full rule
    • For a state with no institute, the entry may name the one body that comes closest. It explains which government designation or qualifying role is missing. Full rule
    • Each state was searched in English and at least one national or official language for a body its government has tasked with testing general-purpose or frontier AI models or named its AI safety or security institute. Bodies listed for context never count as institutes. Full rule
    • Amounts in a currency with an ECB rate are converted to euros at the ECB's 2025 average rates, with no adjustment for inflation or purchasing power, and shown in euros whether or not they are compared. Amounts in a currency the ECB publishes no rate for, such as the Kenyan shilling, stay in that currency and are not compared. Budget and staff figures are rounded to two significant figures, and ~ marks converted figures and figures changed by rounding, except the medians. Full rule
    • We name a head when an official channel of the institute, its host or its government names that person in the role. This includes government directories and official social accounts. Press reports alone do not qualify. Otherwise the row reads Not published. A historical appointment or signature does not by itself confirm continuing tenure. Full rule
    • We show the government body or bodies named as directing or overseeing the institute. This may differ from the organisation that hosts its staff. Joint oversight is shown together. The row does not imply independence, a direct reporting relationship to a minister, or that the host's director also leads the institute. Full rule
    • We list public bodies and public-interest research organisations named by an institute or its government as working with it. A text in force that assigns the body a specific task counts as working with the institute; plans, strategies and future commitments are marked planned. An adopted programme for the current period that assigns the work counts as in force. A body mentioned only as an example in a general duty to cooperate is excluded. Consortium members need separate evidence to be listed individually. Hosts and private firms are excluded. Federation members are labelled members. Full rule
    • We record whether a source says an institute tests AI models itself or through other bodies, and how it gets access to leading developers' models: dated access before public release or deeper access (fewer safeguards, or weights or internals), a legal power to require access, or a published agreement with a developer. Not published means not stated in the sources we searched. Full rule

    Full method

    Evidence and limits

    • All 32 European states were checked one by one.
    • 1303 sources, 1084 of them primary (government, institute or official documents).
    • International network (International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science): 10 members: the UK, France, the EU, United States, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Australia and Kenya. Membership and having an institute are not the same thing: Germany, Malaysia and India have institutes but are not members; Kenya is a member without an established institute.
    • Population and region sources apply to every entry: Eurostat, World Bank, Department of Household Registration, Ministry of the Interior, United Nations Statistics Division. Entry source lists leave them out; the downloads include them.
    • In our search we found no complete, current official tracker. The best other overviews:
      • UK Government, NIST: Official member list of the international network (10 members: states and the EU). Membership is not a list of institutes.
      • Wikipedia: Actively edited and cites primary sources per state; when checked on 16 Oct 2026 it lacked Germany and Spain.
      • CASRAI: Guide to the network only, without citations.
      • artificialintelligenceact.eu: AI Act national authorities, not AISIs; first published 8 Nov 2024, last updated 17 Jun 2026 when checked.
